en: Homage to the Buddha.
O Blessed One,
wherever I may be reborn through my karmas within the perils of existence, may I there become a man, endowed with faith and unimpaired faculties. (1)

He was proficient in all arts and crafts, learned in all treatises, a renouncer of all material things, and turned away from all sensual desires. He possessed a retentive memory, was free from contradiction, and was pleasing to behold for all sentient beings.
One who associates with spiritual friends, is adorned with the thought of awakening,
is perfected in discipline and conduct, pure, remembers past lives, is wise,
fears the performance of evil deeds, and dwells within the sphere of virtuous conduct. (3–4)
Its sphere is the virtuous intention,
and at the end, it has as its basis the ten perfections and unsurpassed gnosis; and at the end, unsurpassed enlightenment.
O Lord, may I attain that which is unshakable and bestows absolute happiness upon the world.
May I have no womanhood, nor servitude, nor folly, nor birth in wretched lands.
May I never hold wrong views; may the appearance of a Buddha never be absent; and may that morality which is not a cause for Buddhahood never be mine.
Let that not be wealth which is not for the enjoyment of others; let there be no refusal to give when one is asked, "Give alms! Give! even if it be only a trifle.
May my enjoyments not be such as cause suffering to sentient beings.
(7) May I never be born into that family where the Buddha is not the deity—whether I am already born, currently being born, or even while remaining in the womb. (8)
In birth after birth, may I never abandon these five things:
merit, wisdom, power, vigor, and the fifth, the thought of awakening.
By whatever means you, O Protector, attained the state of omniscience, [may I likewise attain it].
Therefore he said: "By whatever means possible, may I attain the state of the Lord of Sages.
Devotion to the Buddha, an honest nature toward all sentient beings, loving-kindness, practice in renunciation, turning away from fruits [of merit], and association with Bodhisattvas.
My nature is unshakable, compassionate toward all beings;
I am ever possessed of mercy, endowed with sharp and vast wisdom, born into a noble family, and possess a beautiful body.
May there be the poetry of the Sugata in every birth; enough with further elaboration.
[May there be] skill in speech, long life, noble birth, a man of sharp intellect, a scholar, and unimpaired faculties.
Devoted to you, he is happy, compassionate, gracious, and a true poet;
he respects his mother, is ever devoted to his father, remembers his past lives, is virtuous, righteous in soul, wealthy, intent on giving, and accompanied by spiritual friends. (12)
Zealous, powerful, beloved, highly esteemed, free from all diseases, compassionate toward sentient beings, retentive of what he has heard, pure in intention, and patient;
[he is] free from all calamities.
O Blessed One, as long as the world exists for the arising of its welfare, may I, possessing patience, attain the state of a Buddha;
until then, may I always be adorned with all these very qualities. 13
The *Candragomipraṇidhāna* is completed. || o ||
Instead of the column heading, the new manuscript reads:
*Oṃ, through generosity the yogi is joyful; through ethical discipline he becomes stainless.*
Through patience he becomes Prabhākara; through vigor, Arciṣmān; and he is Puṇyavān.
Through meditation he is Abhimukha and preeminent; through wisdom, he is Sudurjaya.
He becomes Duraṅgama through great skillful means, and Balavān and Acala.
Through his vow he shall be a Sādhu; as Dharmamegha, he possesses wisdom.
As a Jina and Tathāgata, he becomes the eleventh, realized within himself.
May there be auspiciousness!
